section.title: The Oracle against Moab
section.sectionRationale: This movement completes the arc begun with Babylon and Assyria by turning to Moab, Israel's kindred but often hostile neighbor east of the Dead Sea. Unusually, the oracle is soaked in the prophet's own tears rather than mere denunciation, pictures Moab's refugees begging Judah for shelter, and briefly holds out David's throne established in mercy, before Moab's proud boasting is judged as empty and its glory reduced within a set three years.
section.thesis: Even in pronouncing real judgment on Moab, the LORD's prophet weeps for its devastation, and Moab's only true hope, refuge under the house of David established in steadfast love, is precisely what its own pride refuses to seek, leaving its empty boasting to end in the swift, dated collapse the LORD has spoken.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the sudden devastation of Moab's cities and the prophet's own weeping; the plea for refuge and the throne established in mercy under David's line; and the judgment on Moab's pride, dated precisely to three years.

units.label: Moab devastated, and Isaiah weeps
units.note: my heart cries out over Moab

verses.text:
This is the burden against Moab: 
Ar in Moab is ruined, destroyed in a night! Kir in Moab is devastated, destroyed in a night!

Dibon goes up to its temple to weep at its high places. Moab wails over Nebo, as well as over Medeba. 
Every head is shaved, every beard is cut off.

In its streets they wear sackcloth; on the rooftops and in the public squares 
they all wail, falling down weeping.
Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voices are heard as far as Jahaz. Therefore the soldiers of Moab cry out; their souls tremble within.

My heart cries out over Moab; her fugitives flee as far as Zoar, 
as far as Eglath-shelishiyah. With weeping they ascend the slope of Luhith; they lament their destruction on the road to Horonaim.
The waters of Nimrim are dried up, and the grass is withered; the vegetation is gone, and the greenery is no more.
So they carry their wealth and belongings over the Brook of the Willows.

For their outcry echoes to the border of Moab. Their wailing reaches Eglaim; 
it is heard in Beer-elim.
The waters of Dimon are full of blood, but I will bring more upon Dimon, a lion upon the fugitives of Moab and upon the remnant of the land.
Send the tribute lambs to the ruler of the land, from Sela in the desert to the mount of Daughter Zion.
Like fluttering birds pushed out of the nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon:
“Give us counsel; render a decision. Shelter us at noonday with shade as dark as night. Hide the refugees; do not betray the one who flees.

Let my fugitives stay with you; be a refuge for Moab from the destroyer.” 
When the oppressor has gone, destruction has ceased, and the oppressors have vanished from the land,
in loving devotion a throne will be established in the tent of David. A judge seeking {{mishpat5|justice}} and hastening righteousness will sit on it in faithfulness.
We have heard of Moab's pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit, his overflowing arrogance. But his boasting is empty.
Therefore let Moab wail; let them wail together for Moab. Moan for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth, you who are utterly stricken.

For the fields of Heshbon have withered, along with the grapevines of Sibmah. The rulers of the nations have trampled its choicest vines, which had reached as far as Jazer and spread toward the desert. Their shoots had spread out and passed over the sea.
So I weep with Jazer for the vines of Sibmah; I drench Heshbon and Elealeh with my tears. Triumphant shouts have fallen silent over your summer fruit and your harvest.
Joy and gladness are removed from the orchard; no one sings or shouts in the vineyards. No one tramples the grapes in the winepresses; I have put an end to the cheering.
Therefore my heart laments for Moab like a harp, my inmost being for Kir-heres.
When Moab appears on the high place, when he wearies himself and enters his sanctuary to pray, it will do him no good.
This is the message that the LORD spoke earlier concerning Moab.

And now the LORD says, “In three years, as a hired worker counts the years, Moab's splendor will become an object of contempt, with all her many people. And those who are left will be few and feeble.”

mishpat5.gloss: Justice, right judgment. Even within an oracle of judgment against a foreign nation, this word surfaces as the description of the ideal Davidic ruler, a judge who seeks justice, tying Moab's only possible hope of refuge directly to the same righteous kingship promised throughout Isaiah for Israel and, ultimately, all nations.

basic.context: This oracle pronounces devastating judgment on Moab, Israel's neighbor and distant relative east of the Dead Sea, cataloging city after city falling into mourning, wailing, and flight. Remarkably, the prophet himself is moved to tears over this judgment, not merely announcing it with detachment, and the oracle briefly holds out an actual path to safety, refuge under a coming Davidic ruler who governs in justice and mercy, before returning to describe Moab's proud refusal of that path and its consequent, precisely dated collapse within three years.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, historically anchored judgment oracle against an actual neighboring nation, yet it is unusual among the oracles against the nations for its genuine, repeated expressions of prophetic grief, showing that pronouncing deserved judgment and feeling real compassion for those judged are not contradictory. The honest question this passage raises is why Moab, offered actual refuge under David's throne, ends up judged anyway; the answer given directly in 16:6 is that Moab's own pride and empty boasting kept it from actually seeking the shelter that was genuinely available.
basic.originalLanguages: Even in the middle of describing devastation, the oracle names mishpat, justice, as the defining mark of the coming Davidic ruler who could have offered Moab genuine refuge, tying this foreign nation's hope directly to the same righteous kingship theme running throughout Isaiah. The repeated Hebrew verb for weeping and wailing, used of both Moab's own people and of the prophet himself, blurs the line between judge and mourner throughout the passage.
basic.typology: The throne established in mercy under David's line, offering refuge to fleeing foreigners, anticipates the wider biblical pattern of God's kingdom extending shelter to Gentiles who come in humility, fulfilled fully when Christ, David's greater Son, welcomes people of every nation into His kingdom. Moab's proud refusal of available refuge anticipates the New Testament's warnings that pride, not lack of opportunity, is what ultimately keeps people from the salvation genuinely offered them.
basic.christ: The Davidic throne offered as refuge here, established in mercy with a judge who seeks justice and hastens righteousness, finds its full and final fulfillment in Christ, the true Son of David whose kingdom offers actual shelter to all who come to Him in humility, regardless of national origin, exactly as Ruth the Moabitess herself was grafted into David's own line, Ruth 4:13-17, Matthew 1:5. Isaiah's own tears over judged Moab foreshadow Christ's own weeping over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41, showing that God's justice and God's compassion are never at odds, even when judgment must fall.
basic.god: God's judgment on nations is real and serious, yet it is never detached from compassion; the prophet's own tears model a heart that can pronounce deserved judgment while genuinely grieving over its human cost. God also genuinely offers refuge even to a hostile, judged nation, showing His justice always includes a real, if often refused, invitation to mercy.
basic.crossReferences: Ruth 4:13-17 shows a Moabite woman actually welcomed into David's own line generations before this oracle, proof that ethnic origin was never the barrier; pride and unbelief were. Luke 19:41 has Jesus weep over Jerusalem's coming judgment much as Isaiah weeps here over Moab's. Zephaniah 2:8-11 pronounces similar judgment on Moab for its pride and mockery of God's people. Matthew 1:5 lists Ruth the Moabitess in Jesus's own genealogy, a living testimony that God's grace reaches even nations under judgment.
basic.oneStory: This oracle shows both the reality of deserved judgment and the depth of God's compassion even toward those He judges, offering genuine refuge that pride alone refuses. That refuge, a throne established in mercy under David's line, is fulfilled in Christ, whose own ancestry includes a Moabite woman, proof that no nation's history of judgment forecloses the invitation to find shelter in Him.

context.literary:
The oracle against Moab is the longest of the nation oracles so far, and it is unusual in its form. Most of the others are announcements of doom with a few details of ruin. This one is a lament. It is built in four panels. Chapter 15 is a catalogue of grief, a long run of place names, each a station on the road of flight, from Ar and Kir in the north to Zoar and Horonaim in the south, 15:1 to 9. Chapter 16 begins with a plea and a promise, verses 1 to 5, then returns to accusation and grief, verses 6 to 12, and closes with a dated postscript, verses 13 and 14.

The geography is the structure. The reader is carried along the country from town to town, and nearly every verse has a name and a sound of weeping. The stress is on speed and suddenness: 'destroyed in a night,' 15:1, spoken twice. The root behind 'destroyed' in 15:1 is the one behind 'the destroyer' in 16:4, so the opening disaster and the refugees' plea are tied by a single word.

The centre of the whole piece is 16:4b to 5, the promise of a throne. The oracle moves from ruin to a single sentence about the tent of David and then back to ruin. A reader who skips it will find a record of an unhappy nation; a reader who stops there will find the hinge of the passage. 'In loving devotion a throne will be established in the tent of David,' and the promise is set among pictures of burned fields and silent winepresses.

The voice also changes. In 15:5 and 16:9 to 11 the speaker is the prophet or the LORD, and it is a speaker who weeps. Elsewhere in the oracles against the nations the voice is cold. Here Isaiah's heart cries out, his tears drench the vineyards, and his inmost being laments like a harp. The literary effect is to make the judgment felt.

The passage ends with a clock. Verse 13 says what the LORD had spoken 'earlier,' and verse 14 adds 'And now,' fixing a term of three years. That shows the oracle came in two layers, an earlier word and a later one with a date.
context.historical:
Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, on the plateau between the Arnon river and the Wadi Zered, with Ammon to the north and Edom to the south. Its people traced their descent to Lot, Genesis 19:37, and the relationship with Israel was close and fraught. God told Israel not to harass the Moabites, since He had given Ar to the descendants of Lot, Deuteronomy 2:9, yet the nation hired Balaam to curse Israel, Numbers 22 to 24, and was excluded from the assembly 'even to the tenth generation,' Deuteronomy 23:3 to 4. Moab's king Eglon oppressed Israel in the days of the judges, Judges 3:12 to 14, and in the ninth century King Mesha, who 'rendered' a hundred thousand lambs to Israel and then rebelled, 2 Kings 3:4 to 5, set up a stone that survives, recording his own account of these events.

Yet the relationship also had tenderness. Ruth was a Moabite woman, Ruth 1:4, and became the great-grandmother of David, Ruth 4:17. David left his parents under the protection of the king of Moab when he was in flight, 1 Samuel 22:3 to 4. The plea of 16:4, 'Let my fugitives stay with you,' is almost the language David used in Moab.

The cities of Isaiah 15 are mainly those of the plateau north of the Arnon, in territory once given to Reuben and Gad, Numbers 32:3 and 37 to 38: Heshbon, Elealeh, Nebo, Medeba, Dibon. Moab had retaken them. The vineyards of Heshbon and Sibmah were famous, and the wine was a pillar of the economy, 16:8 to 10.

Moab's own religion is the setting for 15:2 and 16:12. Its god was Chemosh, Numbers 21:29 and 1 Kings 11:7, and its people went up to high places and sanctuaries to weep and to pray. The oracle says that when Moab 'wearies himself' at the sanctuary, it 'will do him no good,' 16:12.

The political setting is the Assyrian period. Assyrian royal records list Moab among kingdoms paying tribute, and the oracle's 'in three years' belongs to a time when an Assyrian army, or its allies, could reach the plateau. The passage does not name the invader, and the details are not secure enough to date the three years with confidence.
context.canonical:
The oracle is closely tied to other prophets. Jeremiah 48 reuses much of it. Isaiah 16:6 and Jeremiah 48:29 to 30 share almost the same words, 'We have heard of Moab's pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit,' and Jeremiah 48:31 to 32 repeats the lament for Kir-heres and the vine of Sibmah, with his own 'I will wail for Moab.' A second prophet, a century later, takes Isaiah's tears as his own, and then adds a sentence that closes the whole chapter: 'Yet in the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity,' Jeremiah 48:47.

Moab has a place in the prophets' sense of justice. Amos condemns Moab for burning to lime the bones of Edom's king, Amos 2:1; Zephaniah condemns its taunting of God's people and says it will become like Sodom, Zephaniah 2:8 to 9. Isaiah 25:10 to 12, which follows the song of salvation, uses Moab as the picture of pride: 'his pride will be brought low, despite the skill of his hands.' So Isaiah's own book has Moab twice, once weeping and once in the dust.

The Davidic throne of 16:5 is anchored in 2 Samuel 7:16, 'your throne will be established forever,' and in Isaiah 9:7 and 11:3 to 5, where the child-king reigns in justice and judges the poor with righteousness. Proverbs 20:28 says a king's throne is 'upheld by loving devotion,' a link to the word 'loving devotion' here.

The New Testament takes up both strands. Ruth the Moabitess is named in Jesus' genealogy, Matthew 1:5, and Acts 15:16 to 17 quotes Amos about David's fallen tent being rebuilt so that 'all the Gentiles who are called by My name' may seek the Lord. Jesus weeps over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41, with the same grief that Isaiah has for Moab. The prophets' promise that Gentile nations would find shelter in David's house is explicit in Isaiah 55:5 and is what Paul preaches in Ephesians 2:13 to 14.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted his hearers to see judgment and compassion held together in the same heart. Judah had a long and bitter history with Moab, and a natural response to hearing that Moab would be ruined would be satisfaction. Isaiah does not allow it. He weeps. The hearers were to learn that God's justice on a nation is not delight in its pain, and that those who speak for God ought to speak with tears.

He also meant to show the real offer behind the sentence. The plea of 16:3 and 4 is a genuine opportunity: refugees from Moab are invited, in effect, to come to Zion and take shelter under a throne of 'loving devotion' and justice. Isaiah is telling Judah what kind of kingdom it was meant to be, a place where the hunted could find shelter, where the throne was 'established' on mercy, and the judge was 'hastening righteousness.' Those hearing it were meant to ask whether their own king and city lived up to the description.

Finally, he wanted to explain why the sentence falls. Verse 6 gives the reason: pride. Moab did not lack a way of escape. Its trust was in itself, in its vineyards, in its high places, and in boasts that Isaiah calls empty. The passage warns Judah against the same spirit. A nation or a person that has been told where refuge is and goes elsewhere, because of pride, chooses the outcome.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what God says will happen to Moab and how the prophet feels about it. It does not instruct Israel to attack Moab, and it does not say that the sorrow of the destroyed is something to enjoy. The strong language of 15:9, where God will bring 'more' upon Dimon, is a report of what He will do, not a model for how His people are to treat any neighbour.

The tears are the part meant to carry over. Believers are not told to weep for a nation by decree, but the example is there for those who speak God's warnings. Jeremiah and Jesus both do it, and Paul says he has 'deep sorrow and unceasing anguish' for those who reject the Messiah, Romans 9:2. Anyone who talks about judgment ought to do so with a broken heart, not an eager one.

It is also instructive about refuge. Moab was told where the shelter lay. The principle for readers is that the offer of safety is real and that pride is what usually stops people from taking it. That is true of nations and of individuals. It would be a mistake, though, to read 16:5 as a political programme for any modern state. The throne described is the Lord's, and the offer is first of all a statement about who He is.

debates.question: Whose voice weeps in 15:5 and 16:9 to 11?

views.label: The prophet Isaiah
views.case: The first-person language is natural for a prophet, and Isaiah elsewhere says he weeps for the destruction of 'the daughter of my people,' 22:4. Jeremiah, who echoes this passage, weeps in the same way, Jeremiah 9:1 and 48:31. On this reading the prophet's tears are a model of how a messenger of judgment should feel.

views.label: The LORD Himself
views.case: In 16:9 the speaker says 'I weep... I drench Heshbon and Elealeh with my tears,' and in 16:10 'I have put an end to the cheering,' and in 15:9 'I will bring more upon Dimon.' The same voice who makes the vineyards fail also weeps for them, which suggests that it is God who grieves over what He judges. Other texts show a God who is moved, Hosea 11:8 and Isaiah 63:9.

views.label: Both together
views.case: The prophet is the mouthpiece of God. When he weeps, he expresses God's heart, and the oracle moves seamlessly between the two. This is how prophetic speech often works, and the tears are at once Isaiah's and the LORD's.

debates.bearing: Any of the three views leaves the main point standing: the judgment is not cold. The third view fits how prophets speak and how Scripture describes God, who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, Ezekiel 33:11.

debates.question: Who is the ruler of 16:5, and is the offer genuine?

views.label: A near king of David's line, such as Hezekiah
views.case: The setting is the Assyrian period, and 'the tent of David' could describe the dynasty as ruled in Isaiah's day. Hezekiah was a king who sought the LORD, and some of Moab's refugees may have come to Judah. On this view the verse describes a hope for a good king in the present.

views.label: The Messiah
views.case: The language, 'a judge seeking justice and hastening righteousness,' echoes the Branch of 11:1 to 5 and the king of 9:7, and 'established' recalls the promise of 2 Samuel 7:16 that the throne will be established forever. This is more than any ordinary king did, and Christian readers have long seen it fulfilled in Christ.

views.label: Both, as promise and its first instalment
views.case: A faithful king of David's line would be a first fulfilment, but the full measure of the promise points beyond him to the one who is greater than David.

debates.bearing: The best fit is the third. Isaiah's hearers could take comfort in a king who modelled the promise, and the New Testament shows where it comes to rest. The offer of refuge is real in either case, since the verse describes a throne that welcomes the hunted.

study.originalLanguages:
The passage is thick with words whose sense is lost in translation.

First, the opening burden says that Ar and Kir are 'destroyed in a night.' The verb is shadad, and the cities are 'ruined,' nidmah, from a root that carries the sense of being cut off or silenced. The word shadad returns in 16:4 as shod, 'destruction,' and shoded, 'the destroyer,' so that the refugees pleading for shelter at the fords of the Arnon are fleeing the very thing named in the first line. Two verses at opposite ends of the oracle are held together by one root.

Second, in 15:5 Isaiah says 'My heart cries out over Moab.' The verb is za'aq, to cry out in distress, which describes the cry of the oppressed, as in Exodus 2:23 of Israel in Egypt. It is the verb of people who call for help. The prophet uses for Moab the word that describes Israel's cry in slavery. In 16:11 the same feeling is put in bodily terms: 'my inmost being laments like a harp,' using me'ay, 'my bowels,' the seat of deep feeling, and kinnor, the harp, so that the grief sounds like music played on his own body.

Third, 16:5 piles up the terms of just rule. 'Loving devotion' is chesed, the covenant love that the BSB footnote says includes 'love, goodness, kindness, faithfulness, and mercy, as well as loyalty to a covenant.' The throne is 'established,' from kun, the verb of firmness used in the promise to David, and in 'faithfulness,' emet, which means reliability and truth. The judge 'seeks justice,' mishpat, and 'hastens righteousness,' tsedeq. 'Hastening' is a word that means being swift or skilled. The king does not delay righteousness. The expression 'tent of David' is ohel David, a humble word for a house, perhaps a reminder that the dynasty began in a tent and a shepherd.

Fourth, verse 6 names Moab's sin with a cluster of words from the root of pride, ga'on and ga'avah, together with 'conceit' and 'arrogance,' and says 'his boasting is empty,' using bad, which carries the sense of idle talk or vain words. Jeremiah repeats the cluster, Jeremiah 48:29 to 30. The sin is not a single crime but a cast of mind in which self-reliance fills the whole picture.

Fifth, the dating in verse 14 says 'in three years, as a hired worker counts the years.' The phrase refers to the exact term of a hired labourer's contract, who serves his time neither longer nor shorter and counts the days. The sentence therefore means a precise period. The word for 'splendor' is kavod, glory, the word for the weight of a person's honour, which is to be 'an object of contempt,' qalah, to be made light. Glory becomes lightness, and the nation that was full of itself is emptied.

Sixth, in 15:9 the waters of Dimon are 'full of blood,' dam. Many readers hear a play on the name, since Dimon sounds like the Hebrew for blood. Whether or not the pun is intended, the sound carries the point that the stream is red.

typology.type: A throne established in loving devotion, 16:5
typology.fulfillment: The throne in the tent of David is the promise of 2 Samuel 7:16 and Isaiah 9:7. In the New Testament the angel tells Mary that the Lord God will give her son 'the throne of His father David,' and that 'His kingdom will never end,' Luke 1:32 to 33. The correspondence is that the king described has the covenant love and justice of the promised son of David. The escalation is that He is also 'the Son of the Most High.' The type falls short because every actual king in David's line failed, and this one cannot.

The plea of Moab's refugees, 'Hide the refugees... be a refuge for Moab from the destroyer,' sets out what Zion is for. David had sought such shelter in Moab, 1 Samuel 22:3 to 4, and the tables turn: the nation that once sheltered David asks for shelter at his house. In Christ the invitation is open to all: 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened,' Matthew 11:28. Paul says that those who were once far away have been 'brought near through the blood of Christ,' Ephesians 2:13. The type falls short in that Isaiah gives the refuge a location, while Christ is the refuge in person.

The prophet's compassion for Moab is anticipated by a Moabite woman who took refuge under the wings of Israel's God, Ruth 2:12, and became the mother of the line of David, Ruth 4:17. Matthew names her in the genealogy of Jesus, Matthew 1:5. The correspondence is that Moab's hope is the same as Ruth's: to be gathered into David's house. The escalation is that her great-grandson's greater Son brings people of every nation, Revelation 7:9. The type falls short because Ruth was one woman, and the invitation of the gospel is to all.

Isaiah weeps over a people who deserve judgment. Jesus, approaching Jerusalem, 'wept over it,' Luke 19:41, and cries 'how often I have longed to gather your children together... but you were unwilling,' Matthew 23:37. The correspondence is the heart that grieves over the one it judges. The escalation is that Jesus is not only the messenger but the Judge, and the One who bears the judgment, Hebrews 4:15 to 16. The type falls short because Isaiah's tears could not turn aside the sentence, while the tears of Christ were followed by the cross.

study.christ:
The oracle leads to Christ first by promise, in the single sentence at its centre. 'In loving devotion a throne will be established in the tent of David. A judge seeking justice and hastening righteousness will sit on it in faithfulness,' 16:5. The throne is the one promised in 2 Samuel 7:16, the child-king of Isaiah 9:7 who will 'establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness,' and the Branch of 11:3 to 5 who judges the poor with righteousness. When the angel tells Mary that her son will receive 'the throne of His father David,' Luke 1:32, the hope that Isaiah wrote among the ruins of Moab is announced as arriving. What is striking is the setting. The promise of the great king is given in an oracle about a foreign nation, and the verse says that this king's throne will be a place of shelter for the hunted.

It leads to Christ by the open door. The refugees of Moab ask to be hidden, and the throne that answers is one of chesed. Under the old covenant Moabites were barred from the assembly, Deuteronomy 23:3, yet the prophets look to a day when foreigners will be welcomed, Isaiah 56:3 to 7. In Christ the barrier is removed: 'He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility,' Ephesians 2:14. Jeremiah, who takes up this oracle, ends his judgment on Moab with a promise, 'in the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity,' Jeremiah 48:47, and Paul explains how Gentiles are grafted in to the people of God. Ruth, the Moabite woman in David's line, Matthew 1:5, is the first sign that the door is open. Her great-grandson's great Son is the one who, lifted up from the earth, 'will draw everyone to Myself,' John 12:32.

It leads to Christ by the tears. Isaiah's weeping is unusual among the prophets of the nations. In Jesus it becomes the open grief of God in a human life. 'He wept over it,' Luke 19:41, and He says 'how often I have longed to gather your children together,' Matthew 23:37. Isaiah 42:3, 'a bruised reed He will not break,' is fulfilled in Him, Matthew 12:20, with the added line that 'He will proclaim justice to the nations,' Matthew 12:18. The prophet who weeps over Moab and the Servant who brings justice to the nations belong together.

It leads to Christ by contrast with Moab's pride. Verse 6 says that Moab's trouble is not that no refuge was offered but that it would not stoop to take it. Jesus says the same of Jerusalem, 'you were unwilling,' Matthew 23:37, and teaches 'Blessed are the poor in spirit,' Matthew 5:3. Moab's boast is the opposite of the posture the gospel requires.

A caution keeps the reading honest. This is an oracle about a real nation at a real time, and its promises of a throne were first heard in the world of Hezekiah's Judah. The links to Christ rest on the New Testament's own use of David's throne, of Ruth, and of the tears of Jesus. They do not make every verse of Isaiah 15 a coded gospel.
study.god:
This oracle teaches that God is just and that His justice is not hard. He judges Moab for pride, and the judgment is spelled out in cities and vineyards. Nothing in the passage softens the sentence, and it ends with a deadline. A God who never judged would not be the God of the Bible. The judgment is also measured. It follows an offence, 'We have heard of Moab's pomposity,' and it falls in a time of God's choosing.

He grieves. The voice of 16:9 says 'I weep,' and in 16:11 'my inmost being' laments for Moab. The oracle does not describe a God who regrets His own decision, for the sentence stands, but one who feels the loss it brings. The same God who said 'I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked,' Ezekiel 33:11, is the one who puts an end to the cheering in the vineyards. The passage holds together two things the Bible always holds together, that He judges and that He is moved. It does not resolve them by making Him less than either.

He is just toward nations. The oracle concerns a people outside the covenant, and the God of Israel treats them as accountable. Moab is not judged for failing to keep the law of Moses but for its pride, its trust in itself, its empty boasting. God holds every people to account for what they know, and the doctrine here is that the LORD is the God of all nations and not only of Israel. This is the same teaching as Paul's in Romans 1 and 2.

He offers refuge. The plea in 16:3 and 4 is not scorned. The passage describes a throne established in loving devotion, and the tone is that of an open door. God does not wait for Moab to be perfect before He offers shelter. The offer of mercy is made even to a nation that has been hostile, and the failure is Moab's. That is the pattern of Jonah 4:11, where God says He cares for Nineveh, and of Isaiah 55:5, where nations who do not know Israel will run to her.

He keeps His word to the day. 'In three years, as a hired worker counts the years.' The precision of the date shows that the God who spoke earlier is the God who fixes the term now. His word is trustworthy in small details as in large ones.

For worship, the passage asks us to treat judgment and compassion as inseparable. Those who speak of God's justice should do so with the tears that Isaiah shows, and those who speak of God's mercy should not forget that pride keeps people from it. It also asks for humility before a God whose refuge is open to all and whose throne is established on faithfulness. We are the people who have been told where shelter lies, and the only thing that can keep us from it is the thing Moab would not give up.

crossReferences.note: Jeremiah reuses Isaiah's oracle, 'We have heard of Moab's pomposity,' and the lament for Kir-heres and the vine of Sibmah, and then ends with a promise of restoration. The two prophets show that this oracle was treasured and applied again. Jeremiah's last line shows where the tears lead: 'In the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity.'

God tells Israel not to harass Moab because He has given Ar to the descendants of Lot. Ar is the first city named in Isaiah 15:1. The ruin of a city God had once protected shows that His judgment is not for lack of earlier care, and that He remembers gifts He gave to other nations.

Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder who rendered a hundred thousand lambs to Israel and then rebelled. The 'tribute lambs' of Isaiah 16:1 may recall this, so that sending the lambs to Zion would mean returning to the old subject relationship, now to the house of David.

David, in flight from Saul, leaves his father and mother in the care of the king of Moab. The plea of Moab's fugitives in Isaiah 16:4, 'Let my fugitives stay with you,' reverses the roles, and Moab asks of David's house what David once asked of Moab.

Ruth the Moabitess becomes the mother of Obed and the great-grandmother of David. The prophecy of a throne in the tent of David that offers refuge to Moab reads differently once the reader knows that David's own line has Moabite blood. Moab is not only a stranger to David's house; it is part of it.

In the song of salvation chapter, Moab is trampled down 'as straw is trodden into the dung pile,' and his pride is brought low. The two oracles complement each other: the same pride that Isaiah 16:6 describes is brought down in 25:11, and the God who weeps over Moab is the God who humbles him.

Moab and Ammon are condemned for taunting God's people, and the sentence is given as the reward for pride. The prophet's view of Moab is stern and shows how the long history of hostility looks to God. It also shows how the compassion of Isaiah 15 and 16 should be read as the other side of a real offence.

The throne 'established' in the tent of David in Isaiah echoes the promise to David that his throne will be established forever. The link makes clear that the king of Isaiah 16:5 is a son of the covenant promise, not a new idea, and that the nations' hope depends on that promise.

Jesus approaches Jerusalem and weeps over it, saying that the city did not recognise the time of its visitation. It is the New Testament parallel of Isaiah's tears, the same grief for a people who would not seek refuge where God provided it. Jesus is both the Judge and the one who weeps.

Gentiles who were 'far away' have been brought near, and the dividing wall is torn down. What Isaiah 16:3 to 5 describes in prospect, a throne where strangers find shelter, Paul describes as accomplished in Christ, so that foreigners are fellow citizens and members of God's household.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with one family and soon divides it into nations. Genesis 10 and 11 give the line from Noah to Babel, and Moab appears in Genesis 19 as the son of Lot. The story of the nations is the story of peoples who have walked away from the God who made them, and the question of the whole Bible is whether any of them can be gathered back. Isaiah 15 and 16 is a short, honest chapter in that story: it shows a nation that is judged and wept over, and a throne that stands ready to receive it.

The passage answers questions raised earlier. When God called Abraham, He said that in him 'all the families of the earth' would be blessed, Genesis 12:3. Moab, a cousin nation with a mixed history, is a test case. The answer here is that the door is not shut by history. Ruth the Moabitess comes in, Jeremiah promises restoration, and Isaiah weeps. Even a nation that has hired Balaam and taunted God's people can be offered shelter.

It also sets up what follows. The oracles against the nations proceed to Damascus, Cush, Egypt, Tyre, and the whole earth, and they end in chapters 24 to 27 with a vision of the world judged and then feasting on the mountain of the LORD, 25:6 to 8, where every tear is wiped away. Isaiah 25:10 to 12 returns to Moab to show pride humbled; chapter 56 promises that foreigners who join themselves to the LORD will not be excluded; chapter 55 calls nations to run to Israel. The tears of 16:9 are answered by the wiped tears of 25:8.

In the larger story the throne of 16:5 is established when Christ is raised and seated at God's right hand. The Gentiles who 'seek the Lord' in Acts 15:17 are the harvest of David's rebuilt tent. The invitation to come, once spoken to a single nation, is made to every people, and the middle wall of partition is broken, Ephesians 2:14. The church lives in the time of the open door and the closed door both, since pride still keeps some from entering.

The story ends with the nations gathered. John sees a multitude 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue' before the throne, Revelation 7:9, and the nations walk by the light of the city, 21:24. The grief that Isaiah felt for Moab is answered there: God Himself will wipe away every tear, and the throne of the Lamb, the true son of David, rules in justice and loving devotion forever. What the passage showed as a promise at the edge of ruin is seen in the end as a city whose gates are never shut.

quiz.q: What is unusual about the prophet's own tone in pronouncing this judgment on Moab?

options.text: Isaiah repeatedly expresses his own genuine grief and tears over Moab's devastation, rather than detached denunciation.
options.note: Phrases like 'my heart cries out over Moab' and 'I weep with Jazer' are distinctive within these oracles against the nations.

options.text: Isaiah expresses joy and celebration over Moab's fall.
options.note: The tone is one of genuine sorrow and weeping, not celebration.

options.text: Isaiah refuses to pronounce any judgment on Moab at all.
options.note: The judgment is pronounced clearly and repeatedly; what is unusual is the accompanying grief, not an absence of judgment.

options.text: Isaiah blames Judah, not Moab, for the coming devastation.
options.note: The oracle is explicitly against Moab and its own pride, not primarily an indictment of Judah.

quiz.q: What refuge does 16:3-5 briefly offer to Moab's fleeing refugees?

options.text: Shelter under a throne established in mercy in David's line, governed by a judge who seeks justice.
options.note: This is a real, offered path to safety within the very oracle announcing judgment.

options.text: A permanent military alliance with Assyria.
options.note: The refuge offered is specifically under David's throne, not an Assyrian alliance.

options.text: Full independence and self-rule for Moab.
options.note: The offer is refuge and shelter under Judah's Davidic throne, not Moabite independence.

options.text: Relocation to Egypt.
options.note: The refuge described is specifically 'in the tent of David,' not Egypt.

quiz.q: Why, according to 16:6, does Moab ultimately fail to find lasting safety despite the refuge offered?

options.text: Moab's own pride, conceit, and empty boasting kept it from actually seeking that shelter.
options.note: The text explicitly names pomposity, pride, conceit, and arrogance as the barrier, not any lack of available mercy.

options.text: The offer of refuge was never actually genuine.
options.note: The offer in 16:3-5 reads as a real, if brief, window of genuine hope, not a false promise.

options.text: Moab was geographically too far away to reach Judah.
options.note: The text focuses on pride as the barrier, not geographic distance.

options.text: Judah actively refused to shelter any Moabite refugees.
options.note: The text portrays Judah as being asked for refuge; the failure named is Moab's own pride, not Judah's refusal.

quiz.q: How does Ruth the Moabitess's story relate to this oracle's themes?

options.text: She was actually welcomed into David's own line generations earlier, proving ethnicity was never the true barrier to God's mercy.
options.note: Ruth 4:13-17 and Matthew 1:5 show a Moabite woman fully included in the Messianic line, in striking contrast to Moab's pride here.

options.text: She represents Moab's total and permanent exclusion from God's people.
options.note: Ruth's story shows the opposite: full inclusion and welcome into Israel and David's own family line.

options.text: She has no connection to Isaiah's message about Moab at all.
options.note: Her story provides a striking, directly relevant contrast to Moab's pride-driven refusal of refuge in this oracle.

options.text: She was a queen who ruled over Moab and Judah jointly.
options.note: Ruth was a widow who joined Naomi and later married Boaz, becoming David's great-grandmother, not a ruling queen.

quiz.q: What precise timeframe does 16:14 give for Moab's coming humiliation?

options.text: Three years, counted as precisely as a hired worker counts his years of labor.
options.note: This specific, dated prophecy resembles other precisely timed predictions elsewhere in Isaiah, like the naming of Maher-shalal-hash-baz.

options.text: An immediate, same-day judgment.
options.note: The text specifies a three-year timeframe, not an immediate event.

options.text: Seventy years, echoing the later Babylonian exile timeframe.
options.note: The seventy-year figure belongs to a different, later prophecy regarding Babylon, not this three-year Moab oracle.

options.text: An indefinite, unspecified future period.
options.note: The text is unusually specific, naming three years exactly, not leaving the timing vague.

questions: Isaiah wept even while pronouncing deserved judgment on Moab. Where do you need to hold together honesty about real consequences with genuine compassion for those experiencing them?

Moab was offered real refuge under David's throne but its own pride kept it from seeking that shelter. Where might pride be keeping you from actually receiving help or grace that is genuinely available to you?

Ruth the Moabitess was welcomed fully into David's own family line despite her nation's history under judgment. How does her story encourage you regarding your own past or background that you may feel disqualifies you from God's grace?

The three-year timeframe shows God's judgments are not vague threats but specific and certain. How does that same certainty about God's word encourage you regarding promises He has made that you are still waiting to see fulfilled?

This oracle holds together real judgment and real compassion in a single prophetic voice. Who in your life is under some form of deserved consequence right now, and how can you extend genuine compassion to them without minimizing the reality of what they are facing?

translationNotes.note: 'Destroyed in a night' emphasizes the suddenness of Moab's coming devastation, likely referring to a swift military campaign rather than a single literal overnight event.

'Send the tribute lambs' reflects Moab's historical practice of paying tribute to Judah in livestock, referenced also in 2 Kings 3:4, showing an established, if strained, political relationship between the two nations.

'As a hired worker counts the years' suggests an exact, non-negotiable timeframe, since a hired laborer counts his contracted term precisely rather than loosely, emphasizing the certainty and specificity of this three-year prophecy.
